summary: For ages 10–11: divide numbers up to 4 digits by a two-digit divisor using formal short division where appropriate, choose between short and long division based on how 'friendly' the divisor is, and interpret remainders according to context (as a whole number, fraction, or decimal). The core new skill is strategic METHOD SELECTION once both methods are secure, supported by mental multiples of the divisor and by estimating and checking with multiplication.
misconceptions: Forcing short division with an awkward divisor and making mental-multiple errors (should choose long division).
Carry/remainder errors in the compressed steps because the mental multiplication is insecure.
Not interpreting the remainder appropriately for the context.
Believing one method is always 'better' rather than choosing by the numbers.
Place-value slips when the divisor doesn't fit into a leading digit.

activities.title: Method-chooser: the same division, two ways
steps: Solve 3648÷16 using short division ('bus stop' layout), using a list of multiples of 16 (16, 32, 48, 160, 1600, …) to support the multiply-subtract step at each place.
Solve the SAME calculation 3648÷16 using long division, writing out each multiply-subtract step.
Compare the two side by side and state which was quicker for THIS divisor and why.
Now try a divisor many learners find awkward, e.g. 4080÷17, by short division; notice whether and where holding multiples of 17 mentally becomes error-prone.
Solve 4080÷17 again by long division and compare how reliable each felt.
State a rule of thumb in your own words: when the divisor's multiples are easy to hold, short division is efficient; when they are hard, long division is safer.
Estimate first (e.g. 3600÷16 ≈ 225) and check the final answer by multiplying the quotient back (228×16 = 3648?).
activities.insight: Whether short or long division is the better tool depends on how friendly the divisor is, not on habit — and you can experience this trade-off by doing the same calculation both ways. Both methods are legitimate; the skill is choosing and justifying.

activities.title: Justify the method for a mixed set
steps: For each calculation in a mixed set (e.g. 3648÷16, 4080÷17, 2925÷15, 5887÷29), decide whether short or long division suits it before computing.
Write one sentence explaining your choice, referring to whether the divisor's multiples are easy to derive.
Carry out the division with your chosen method, then estimate and check by multiplying back.
Answer: is any ONE method always 'better'? Explain why not, using an example from your set.
activities.insight: Strategic tool choice means matching the method to the numbers; no single method is universally superior, and whether a divisor is 'friendly' depends on which multiples you can derive quickly.

activities.title: Interpreting the remainder in context
steps: Solve a measurement problem where the remainder must be expressed appropriately, e.g. '5 m of ribbon is shared into 16 equal pieces — how long is each piece?'
Share the leftover too: remainder over divisor gives the fraction of a metre added to each piece (here 5/16 m), then convert it to a decimal length.
For a different context (e.g. buses needed to carry people, or full boxes that can be filled), decide whether to round up, round down, or keep a remainder, and explain why.
Use a bar model or number line to show what the leftover represents before writing it as a fraction/decimal.
activities.insight: A remainder is not always written as 'r n' — the context dictates whether it becomes a fraction, a decimal, or forces rounding, so you must interpret what the leftover means.

activities.title: Check your understanding
steps: Choose: for 3648÷16 versus 4080÷17, which calculation better suits short division, and give the reason.
Fill in the missing step of a partially worked short-division ('bus stop') layout, including writing a zero in the quotient where the divisor doesn't fit a place.
Select the correctly interpreted remainder for a measurement context (e.g. the length of each piece as a fraction or decimal) rather than a whole-number 'r' form.
activities.insight: You can recognise the appropriate method, execute a short-division step correctly, and interpret a remainder for its context.

checkQuestion: Ask the child to compute 3,648 ÷ 16 while you watch, letting them choose their method. Then give a measurement division whose remainder must be expressed as a fraction or decimal (e.g. '5 m of ribbon shared into 16 equal pieces — how long is each?') and watch how they handle the remainder. Notice whether they lean on multiples of the divisor and how they interpret what's left over.
checkAnswer: 3,648 ÷ 16 = 228 (exact). For 5 m ÷ 16, each piece is 0.3125 m (or 5/16 m). The teacher watches for a workable division method (chunking known multiples of 16, or short/long division) and correct interpretation of the remainder as a fraction/decimal rather than 'r something' when the context demands it.
